newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Far East Gold - IMF bearish, lease rates worrying.
newsitem.headline: Far East Gold - IMF bearish, lease rates worrying.

text.p: News the International Monetary Fund (IMF) board has enough votes to approve gold sales has dented prices in the short term, but increased borrowing of the metal is a more significant market factor, bullion traders said on Friday.

Senior Hong Kong-based gold traders dismissed the IMF announcement by chief Michael Camdessus as a "non-event," noting that the market had largely absorbed the news but that sentiment was still shaky.
"I really don't think in the longer run it will have much of an impact on the market," said Dickran Gazmararian, Asia Pacific executive vice-president of precious metals for Republic National Bank.

Gold was quoted at $380.60/$381.10 an ounce in Hong Kong around midday on Friday, down slightly from the previous New York close of $380.90/$381.40, but above Thursday afternoon's London fix at $380.45 -- the lowest since September 5, 1995.
The slump followed comments by Camdessus that the IMF had garnered enough votes from its members to sell five million ounces of gold from its reserves to relieve the debts of impoverished nations.
Analysts and gold traders said the IMF sale would be carefully conducted over a long period of time and speculators had simply been taking a last minute punt on the metal.

"Gold has gone down because dealers are looking for $377-$378, and it is still very bearish. We're looking for a rally, but I don't think the worst is over yet," said a gold source at an international bank's Hong Kong office.
Hong Kong traders said they were more concerned about tightening gold lease rates than IMF sales.
"There is a lot of physical demand at these levels, which means that there's extra demand on physical supply which puts pressure on lease rates," one said.

One month implied gold lease rates ended around 1.59 percent on Thursday in New York, after moving up sharply from around 1.33 percent early in the day, and closing at 1.47 on Wednesday. Talk in the market that an international Jewish organisation might receive 100 tonnes of Nazi gold stashed in Swiss banks was also making some dealers nervous over the direction of lease rates, other gold sources said.
They said the market feared a repetition of the situation at the end of 1995, when huge amounts of borrowing squeezed the market, sending borrowing rates soaring.

"There's been some producer selling and we see borrowing interest in the short term period, especially overnight," said a gold dealer at a European bank's Hong Kong office, adding, "I think producers sold some gold and they have to finance it."
But Gazmararian said he did not anticipate the market being squeezed as players were borrowing metal to cover themselves for the year-end.
Other senior bullion sources said they would wait before predicting a direction for gold, giving players until the end of the quarter to clear their books and complete housekeeping matters.
"Historically towards the end of the year a lot of central banks ask for their metal back before they lend it back to the market, to assess whether the loans are performing," one gold dealer said.
